title: Concurrency: why "at the same time" is usually a lie

claims.text: Lamport examined the concept of one event happening before another in a distributed system and showed it defines a partial ordering of the events, in Communications of the ACM in 1978, volume 21, pages 558 to 565. He gives a distributed algorithm for synchronising a system of logical clocks which can be used to totally order the events, and then specialises it for physical clocks, deriving a bound on how far out of synchrony they can become.

source.title: Leslie Lamport, Time, clocks, and the ordering of events in a distributed system, Communications of the ACM 21(7):558-565, July 1978, doi 10.1145/359545.359563

claims.text: The ordering is partial rather than total, and that is the substantive claim. Events can be compared when a causal path connects them, through program order or through message passing, and cannot be compared otherwise. A total order can be recovered only by breaking ties with an arbitrary ordering of the processes, so the partial order is unique while the total order is a convention.

source.title: Leslie Lamport, Time, clocks, and the ordering of events in a distributed system, Communications of the ACM 21(7):558-565, July 1978, doi 10.1145/359545.359563

beats.broke: two things appear to happen at once, and the phrase at the same time presumes a shared clock that no collection of independent machines actually has
beats.fix: order events by causality rather than by time — one event precedes another only if information could have flowed from the first to the second, which gives a partial order that is genuinely defined
beats.cost: a partial order leaves genuinely unrelated events incomparable, so any total ordering you need must be manufactured by an arbitrary tie-break rather than discovered
beats.interview: what it means for two events to happen at the same time on two machines
